column2: Then Asita saw him pass beyond all the stations of the Rudras and Vasus, and of Brihaspati.
Ascending to the world of the cows, he saw Jaigishavya going on to the worlds of those who perform the Brahma sacrificial sessions.
He followed the Brahmana as, by his own energy, he rose to three other worlds, and went to the worlds of devoted wives.
Then Asita no longer saw the best of sages, Jaigishavya, established in yoga, who had vanished, subduer of foes.
Devala, greatly fortunate, reflected on Jaigishavya's power, his firm vows and the incomparable perfection of his yoga.
Then Asita, self-controlled, with joined palms, wise, asked those perfected ones, best in the worlds, who performed the Brahma sessions:
I do not see Jaigishavya; tell me of that greatly energetic one. I wish to hear this, for my curiosity is very great.
[The perfected ones said:] "Hear the truth as we tell it, Devala of firm vows: Jaigishavya has gone to the eternal, imperishable world of Brahma."
Hearing the words of those perfected ones of the Brahma sessions, Asita Devala swiftly sprang up and fell down again.
Then the perfected ones said again to Devala: "Devala, ascetic, you have no path to go there, to the abode of Brahma that Jaigishavya has attained."
Hearing the words of the perfected ones, Devala descended again through all those worlds in order.
He came like a bird to his own holy hermitage, and on entering saw Jaigishavya there.
Then, with a mind joined to dharma, Devala reflected on having seen the power of Jaigishavya's austerity, born of yoga.
Then Devala, bowed in humility, approaching the great sage Jaigishavya, said to him, O king: "Revered one, I wish to take up the dharma of liberation."
Hearing his words, he instructed him in the supreme method of yoga and in what is to be done and not done according to the scriptures.
Seeing him resolved on renunciation, the great ascetic performed all his rites by the method seen in the scriptures.
Seeing him resolved on renunciation, the beings with the ancestors then wept, saying, "Who will share with us?"
Hearing the words of the beings and their piteous cry, Devala, resounding in the ten directions, set his mind to renounce liberation.
Then fruits and roots and sacred things, Bharata, flowers and herbs cried out in thousands:
The petty-minded Devala will surely cut us off again; he does not understand that he gave safety to all beings.
Then the best of sages deliberated again with his own mind: "Which would be better, liberation or the dharma of the householder?"
Having so decided in his mind, O best of kings, Devala gave up the householder's dharma and chose the dharma of liberation.
Reflecting thus and on other matters, Devala from resolve then attained supreme perfection and supreme yoga, Bharata.
Then the gods assembled, led by Brihaspati, and the ascetics praised Jaigishavya and his austerity.
Then the best of sages Narada said to the gods: "There is no austerity in Jaigishavya, who astonishes Asita."
To him who spoke so, the wise one, the dwellers in heaven replied, "Not so," praising the great sage Jaigishavya.
Touching the water there too, the great-souled plough-bearer gave wealth to the Brahmanas and, having gained dharma, performer of supreme deeds, went to the great tirtha of Soma.
Touching the water there too and giving gifts, the self-possessed and righteous Bala went to the tirtha of the sage Sarasvata,
where in a twelve-year drought the sage Sarasvata of old taught the Vedas to the best of Brahmanas.
[Janamejaya said:] "How did the ascetic Sarasvata of old teach the Vedas in the twelve-year drought?"
[Vaishampayana said:] "Of old, great king, there was a wise and greatly ascetic sage famed as Dadhicha, a celibate with senses controlled.
Shakra ever feared his great austerity, lord; he could not be tempted even with fruits of many kinds.
To tempt him, Pakashasana sent the divine, holy and lovely Apsara Alambusha.
As that great soul was offering libations to the gods in the Sarasvati, the lady appeared near him, great king.
Seeing her of divine form, the seed of that sage of purified soul fell into the Sarasvati, and the river received it.
Seeing that seed, bull among men, she took it into her womb, and the great river bore that embryo for the sake of a son.
In due time that best of rivers bore a son, and taking the son she went to the sage, lord.
Seeing that best of sages in the assembly of sages, the river then said, giving him that son: "Brahmin-sage, this is your son, borne by me out of devotion to you.
Seeing the Apsara Alambusha, your seed fell earlier; I bore it in my womb, Brahmin-sage, out of devotion to you.
Resolved that your energy not be lost, accept your own blameless son, given by me."
So told, he accepted him and, the best of the twice-born, was greatly pleased; he smelled his head with mantras and with love.
Embracing him for a long time, best of the Bharatas, the great sage, pleased, then gave the Sarasvati a boon:
The Vishvedevas, ancestors, Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases, fortunate one, being offered libations of your water, will be satisfied.
Having said this, pleased and highly delighted in his soul, he praised the great river with words; hear that duly, O king.

You came forth, greatly fortunate one, from the lake of Brahma of old; sages of keen vows know you, best of rivers.
mahabharata:9:50.20	You are ever one who does what is dear to me, pleasing to behold; therefore your son, fair-complexioned one, shall be great.
mahabharata:9:50.21	Your son, renowned by your very name, sustainer of the worlds, shall be famed as Sarasvata, a great ascetic.
mahabharata:9:50.22	In a twelve-year drought, greatly fortunate one, this Sarasvata will teach the Vedas to the best of Brahmanas.
mahabharata:9:50.23	And you, auspicious one, shall always be the holiest of holy rivers, greatly fortunate Sarasvati, by my grace.
Thus praised by him and having obtained the boon, the great river, glad, took her son and went, bull of the Bharatas.
At this very time, in the strife of gods and Danavas, Shakra, seeking a weapon, wandered through the three worlds.
The revered Shakra found no weapon fit for the slaying of the enemies of the gods.
Then Shakra said to the gods: "I cannot slay the great asuras, foes of the gods, without the bones of Dadhicha.
So go, best of the gods, and beg the best of sages: 'Give us your bones, Dadhicha, that we may slay our foes with them.'"
Begged by the gods for his bones, the best of sages then without hesitation gave up his life, saying "Do so"; and he gained imperishable worlds, having done what the gods loved.
From his bones Shakra, with a delighted mind, had divine weapons made of many kinds: thunderbolts, discuses, maces and many heavy clubs.
For that was formed by the great seer, the son of Prajapati, Bhrigu, sustainer of the worlds, by intense austerity.
Huge-bodied and radiant, made from the essence of the worlds, it came into being, heavy as a mountain, tall, famed for its greatness; Pakashasana is ever disturbed by its energy.
With that thunderbolt, charged with mantras, hurled in great anger, born of Brahma's energy, the revered one slew nine times ninety Daitya and Danava heroes.
Then, after time had passed, a very great and fearful drought came, O king, of twelve years.
In that twelve-year drought the great sages, afflicted by hunger, ran in all directions for sustenance, O king.
Seeing them scattering in all directions, the sage Sarasvata then resolved to go, and the Sarasvati said to him:
You must not go from here, son; I shall always give you food, the best of fish; stay here, Bharata.
So told, he made offerings to the ancestors and gods, and ate daily, sustaining his life and the Vedas.
Then, when that drought had passed, the great sages asked one another again for the sake of Vedic study.
Afflicted by hunger, as they wandered, their Vedas were lost; of them all, O king of kings, none had any readiness.
Then one of those sages came to the best of sages Sarasvata, who was reciting his own Vedic study.
Having gone, he told the others of the radiant Sarasvata, who, like an immortal, was reciting the Veda in a solitary place.
Then all the great sages assembled there, O king, and said this to the best of sages Sarasvata:
Teach us. Then the sage said, "Become my pupils duly."
Then the host of sages said, "You are a boy, son." He told the sages again, "Let my dharma not be lost.
One who teaches unrighteously or takes unrighteously—let both die soon or become enemies.
Not by years, grey hairs, wealth or kinsmen did the sages make dharma; he who has learned the Veda is great among us."
Hearing his words, those sages, having duly obtained the Vedas from him, practised dharma again.
Sixty thousand sages became pupils of the Brahmin-sage Sarasvata for the sake of Vedic study.
Then they all brought handfuls of darbha grass for the seat of the Brahmin-sage, though they stood under the sway of a boy.
Giving wealth there too, the mighty son of Rohini, elder brother of Keshava, glad, went in order to the great famed tirtha where the Old Maiden (Vriddhakanya) was.
This is very hard, Brahmana, and unsurpassed as heard from you; tell the whole truth of how she was established in austerity.

[Vaishampayana said:] "There was a sage of great valour, Kuni Gargya, greatly renowned; having practised vast austerity, O king, that best of ascetics, the lord, begot a mind-born daughter of fair brows.
Seeing her, the greatly renowned Kuni Gargya, greatly pleased, went to heaven, O king, leaving his body here.
The fair-browed, auspicious one, lotus-eyed and blameless, made a hermitage by great and fierce austerity.
Worshipping ancestors and gods with fasts, by her fierce austerity a great barrier was crossed, O king.
Though offered by her father to a husband, the blameless one did not wish it; she saw no husband equal to herself.
Then, afflicting her body with fierce austerity, she devoted herself to worship of ancestors and gods in a lonely forest.
Though she thought herself to have accomplished her task, she was weary, worn by old age and by austerity, O king of kings.
When she could not walk even a step by herself, she then resolved to go to the other world.
Seeing her desiring to leave the body, Narada said: "How can there be worlds for you, blameless one, an unwed maiden without the marriage rite?
Thus we have heard in the world of the gods, great-vowed one: you have attained supreme austerity but have not won the worlds."
Hearing Narada's words, she said in the assembly of sages: "I give half my austerity to whoever takes my hand, good ones."
When this was said, the sage Shringavan, son of Galava, took her hand and first made this condition:
On this condition I shall take your hand today, fair one: that you stay with me for one night.
She agreed, "So be it," and gave him her hand; and the son of Galava performed the hand-taking and the marriage.
In the night, O king, she became a young woman of divine hue, with divine ornaments and garments, and divine garlands and unguents.
Seeing her, as if shining with her own radiance, the son of Galava was pleased; he stayed one night, and in the morning she said to him:
The condition you made with me, Brahmana, best of ascetics, I have lived by; good fortune to you; I go.
Permitted, she said further: "Whoever stays one night composed at this tirtha, satisfying the gods,
shall gain the fruit of properly practising celibacy for forty-eight years and ten years." Having said this, the virtuous woman left her body and went to heaven.
The sage too became wretched, thinking of her beauty; by the condition he had hardly obtained half her austerity.
Perfecting himself, he followed her path, grieved, bull of the Bharatas, drawn by the power of her beauty. This great story of the Old Maiden has been told to you.
Staying there, the plough-bearer heard that Shalya had been slain; giving gifts to the twice-born there too, scorcher of foes, he grieved for Shalya, slain in battle by the Pandavas.
Leaving through the gate of Samantapanchaka, Madhava Rama asked the host of sages about the fruit of Kurukshetra.
Asked by the lion of the Yadus, those great souls told him all about the fruit of Kurukshetra as it was.
Of old this was ploughed for many years by the wise and royal sage, the best of them, of immeasurable energy, the great-souled Kuru; hence it became known here as Kurukshetra.
[Rama said:] "Why was this field ploughed by the great-souled Kuru? I wish to hear this told, ascetics."
[The sages said:] "Of old, it is said, Shakra came from heaven to Kuru, who ever rose up to plough, and asked the reason:
'What is this, O king, with such great effort? What do you intend, royal sage, that you plough this earth?'
[Kuru said:] 'Those men, Shatakratu, who die in this field will go to worlds of merit, free of sin.'
Laughing, the lord Shakra went to heaven, and the royal sage, undismayed, continued to plough the earth.
Coming again and again, Shatakratu laughed at him each time, and having asked the undismayed one, went away again and again.
When by fierce austerity he had ploughed the earth, O king, Shakra told the gods what the royal sage intended.
Hearing that, the gods said to the thousand-eyed one: 'Shakra, if it can be done, dissuade the royal sage with a boon.
For if men here, gladdened, go to heaven without sacrificing to us with rites, we shall have no share.'
Then Shakra came and said to the royal sage: 'Enough of your toil; do as I say.
Men who, fasting, unwearied, give up the body here, or are rightly slain in battle, even animals, O king,
let them share in heaven, O king of kings, great-minded one.' 'So be it,' King Kuru then said to Shakra.
Then, having taken his leave, the slayer of Bala, with a delighted heart, quickly went again to heaven.
Thus, best of the Yadus, this was ploughed of old by the royal sage, and permitted by Shakra: holy for those who give up their lives here.
Here Shakra himself, lord of the gods, sang a verse about Kurukshetra; hear it, plough-bearer.
Even dust raised by the wind from Kurukshetra carries even an evildoer to the highest state.
Divine sages, the best of Brahmanas, and Nriga and other chief kings, tiger among men, having sacrificed with costly rites and laid down their bodies here, have attained a good state.
The region between Tarantuka and Arantuka, the Rama lakes and Machakruka: this is Kurukshetra, Samantapanchaka, called the northern altar of Prajapati.
This is auspicious, great and holy, dear to the gods, endowed with the merits of heaven; therefore all kings of the earth, slain here, will go to the state of great souls."
Filled with madhuka and mango forests, thronged with plaksha and nyagrodha trees, with chiribilva, holy, thronged with jackfruit and arjuna trees,
seeing it, the best of the Yadavas, of excellent holy marks, asked all the sages, "Whose is this excellent hermitage?"
They all said to the great-souled plough-bearer, O king: "Hear in detail, Rama, whose hermitage this was of old.
Here of old the god Vishnu practised supreme austerity; here all his eternal sacrifices were duly performed.
Here a perfected Brahmin woman, a lifelong celibate, joined to yoga, went to heaven, perfected in austerity, an ascetic.
She was the glorious daughter of the great-souled Shandilya, O king, of firm vows, virtuous, restrained and celibate.
Having attained supreme yoga, she went to the unsurpassed heaven; enjoying in the hermitage the fruit of the horse sacrifice, the auspicious one went to heaven, honoured by the self-controlled."
Having visited the holy hermitage and seen it, the bull of the Yadus, Achyuta, saluted those sages, then on the side of the Himalaya sent back all his camps and ascended the mountain.
Having gone not far, the strong palm-bannered one saw a holy, excellent tirtha and was filled with supreme wonder.
Bala reached the source of the Sarasvati, Plakshaprasravana, and the excellent best of tirthas, Karapachana.
The mighty plough-bearer gave gifts there too, bathed in the cool water, and from there went, highly pleased, to the hermitage of Mitra and Varuna,
where Indra, Fire and Aryaman had earlier attained joy. From Karapachana he went to that place on the Yamuna.
Bathing there too, the righteous one, gaining supreme satisfaction, the mighty bull of the Yadus sat with the sages and the perfected, and heard bright stories.
While they were so seated, the revered sage Narada came to that place where Rama was seated.
Wrapped in a mass of matted locks, wearing golden bark, a great ascetic, bearing a golden staff, O king, and a water-pot,
holding that lovely lute, the Kachchhapi vina of pleasant sound, skilled in dance and song, honoured by gods and Brahmanas,
the maker of quarrels, ever fond of quarrels, he came to the place where the glorious Rama sat.
Rising, they all honoured that strict-vowed one, and asked the divine sage what had happened concerning the Kurus.
Then Narada, knower of all dharma, told him, O king, all that had happened, the destruction of the Kurus already past.
Then the son of Rohini said to Narada in a sorrowful voice: "In what state is that kshatriya host, and the kings who were there?
I had heard all this earlier, ascetic, but I have great curiosity to hear it in detail."
[Narada said:] "Bhishma was slain at the beginning, and Drona, and the lord of the Sindhus, and Karna son of Vikartana and his sons, great chariot-warriors.
Bhurishravas, son of Rohini, and the valiant king of the Madras: these and many other mighty ones here and there,
giving up their dear lives for the Kaurava's sake, kings and princes who never turned back in battle.
Hear from me, mighty-armed Madhava, who remain unslain: in the Dhritarashtra host, Kripa, valiant Bhoja and the heroic Ashvatthaman survive, gone to the quarters with their army broken.
With his army slain and Kripa and the others fled, Duryodhana, greatly distressed, entered the lake called Dvaipayana.
As Dhritarashtra's son lay with the water stilled, the Pandavas with Krishna tormented him with fierce words.
Goaded on all sides by words, Rama, the strong hero rose from the lake, taking up a great mace.
He has also now come to battle with Bhima; and that very dreadful fight between the two will be soon, Rama.
If you have curiosity, go, Madhava, without delay; see the great and terrible battle of your two pupils, if you think fit."
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing Narada's words, he honoured those best of Brahmanas and dismissed all who had come with him, saying "Go to Dvaraka," and instructed his followers.
Descending from the best of mountains, from the auspicious Plakshaprasravana, pleased at heart, having heard the great fruit of the tirthas, Achyuta sang this verse in the presence of the Brahmanas:

What delight is equal to dwelling on the Sarasvati? What merits are equal to dwelling on the Sarasvati? People who reach heaven by the Sarasvati will ever remember the river Sarasvati.
mahabharata:9:53.35	The Sarasvati is holy among all rivers, the Sarasvati ever brings happiness to the world; having reached the Sarasvati, people, though great sinners, ever grieve not, here or hereafter.
Then, looking again and again at the Sarasvati with love, the scorcher of foes mounted a bright chariot yoked with horses.
By that swift chariot the bull of the Yadus, eager to see, reached the place where his pupils' battle was at hand.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Seeing Rama present when the mace-fight was at hand, how did my son fight Bhima, Sanjaya?"
[Sanjaya said:] Reaching the presence of Rama, your son Duryodhana, mighty-armed and valiant, eager for battle, rejoiced.
Seeing the plough-bearer, the king rose, Bharata, and, filled with supreme joy, spoke to Yudhishthira:

Let us go quickly from here to Samantapanchaka, lord of men, the renowned northern altar of Prajapati in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:9:54.6	In that most holy, eternal place of the three worlds, whoever meets his death in battle will surely go to heaven.
Saying "So be it," great king, the hero Yudhishthira, son of Kunti, the lord, advanced toward Samantapanchaka.
Then King Duryodhana, radiant, taking up a great mace, went on foot in anger with the Pandavas.
As he went thus, mace in hand and armoured, the gods in the sky honoured him with "Well done, well done," and the men there who were weather-seers were delighted to see him.
Surrounded by the Pandavas, your son, king of the Kurus, went with the gait of a rutting lord of elephants.
Then with the blare of conches, the great sound of kettledrums and the lion-roars of heroes, all the quarters were filled.
Having gone to the western region as indicated by your son, and enclosed on all sides by them,
to the south of the Sarasvati, at the excellent tirtha Svayana, in that barren place they chose to fight.
Having slain those crows, Kaushika (the owl) was glad, having repaid his enemies as he wished, slayer of foes.
Nor should you grieve, O king, for those slain in battle; if the scriptures are authority, they have gone to the highest state.
Seeking the reason for the likeness of Pritha's and yours, however much I think, I cannot find the cause.
[Death said:] "You are to be killed by me, evil-minded one, child-killer, doer of cruelty; why do you say so much, vilest of serpents, who are to be slain?"
And you think yourself a sinner in the end; hear how sin is removed, Bharata.
By that conduct the king was pleased with him, and he repented, remembering his dull and senseless son.
While the Panchajanya sounded in the dwelling of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, asses with dreadful voices brayed on every side in reply.
Then, turning back, they saw the west, and saw Dvaraka submerged by the sea.
Full of gnats, crickets, flies and mosquitoes, encircled on every side by corpses here and there.
